data: World's highest-latitude active orbital launch complex — Russia's polar / Molniya military + GLONASS pad

Soyuz pad at Plesetsk Cosmodrome, 62.9°N — the highest-latitude active orbital launch complex in the world. Originally an R-7 / R-9 ICBM base from the late 1950s; converted to space launches in 1966. Site 43 specifically operates Soyuz-2 today and historically hosted more orbital launches than any single site in the world for several decades. Russia's polar / Molniya / GLONASS workhorse, plus military payloads. The high latitude limits useful inclinations but suits sun-synchronous, Molniya, and high-inclination orbits. Coordinates from Russian Ministry of Defence + Roscosmos public records.
Plesetsk's workhorse Soyuz pad at 62.9°N — the world's highest-latitude active orbital launch complex

Plesetsk Cosmodrome sits at 62.9°N — the world's highest-latitude active orbital launch complex. Site 43 is one of several pads at Plesetsk and operates Soyuz-2 today for Russian polar / Molniya / GLONASS payloads. Originally an R-7 ICBM base in the late 1950s, repurposed for space launches in 1966, and for several decades Plesetsk held the record for most orbital launches from any single site on Earth. The high latitude limits how much the Earth's rotation contributes (less than at Baikonur or Wenchang), but it's perfect for high-inclination missions that Baikonur can't easily reach without dogleg manoeuvres.
